title: Creating Your First Database and Table
description: Write your first CREATE DATABASE and CREATE TABLE statements, define columns with data types and constraints, and insert your first row.

data.text: Now that you understand databases and tables conceptually, it's time to create one. In this lesson you'll create a new database, define a table with columns and a primary key, and insert your first record.
The simplest way to create a new database is with the CREATE DATABASE statement:

data.title: Create a sample database

data.text: After CREATE DATABASE, SQL Server creates the data and log files on disk. The GO command is a batch separator (recognized by SSMS and sqlcmd, not by SQL Server itself). USE switches the current connection to your new database.

data.title: The USE statement
data.text: USE is a session-level command — it changes which database your subsequent statements reference, but only for this connection. Each new query window must specify its own database context.
Every column in a table needs a name and a data type. The most common pattern is to include an integer primary key with the IDENTITY property so SQL Server auto-increments it for each new row.

data.title: Create a customers table
data.code:
CREATE TABLE sales.customers (
    customer_id  INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    first_name   VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL,
    last_name    VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL,
    email        VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    phone        VARCHAR(20),
    city         VARCHAR(50),
    state        CHAR(2),
    created_at   DATETIME2    DEFAULT(GETDATE())
);

data.text:
Let's break down what each part does:

- **INT IDENTITY(1,1)** — an integer that starts at 1 and increments by 1 for each new row. No two customers will share an ID.
- **PRIMARY KEY** — tells SQL Server this column uniquely identifies each row. It also creates a clustered index by default.
- **NOT NULL** — the column must contain a value; blanks are rejected.
- **VARCHAR(50)** — a variable-length text field up to 50 characters.
- **CHAR(2)** — a fixed-length field of exactly 2 characters (useful for state codes).
- **DATETIME2** — a modern date-and-time type with high precision.
- **DEFAULT(GETDATE())** — if you don't specify a value, SQL Server fills in the current date and time automatically.

data.title: Insert a single row
data.code:
INSERT INTO sales.customers (first_name, last_name, email, phone, city, state)
VALUES ('Alice', 'Chen', 'alice@example.com', '555-0100', 'Seattle', 'WA');

data.title: Insert multiple rows at once

data.text: Notice that customer_id and created_at are omitted — the IDENTITY value is generated automatically, and created_at gets its DEFAULT. This is the most common INSERT pattern.

data.title: Select all rows back
data.code:
SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, email, city, state
FROM   sales.customers;

data.title: What you learned
points: CREATE DATABASE makes a new database; GO separates batches; USE sets the active database
CREATE TABLE defines columns with data types; IDENTITY(1,1) auto-increments the primary key
PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies each row; NOT NULL rejects blanks
INSERT adds rows; omit IDENTITY and DEFAULT columns for auto-population
SELECT retrieves and verifies your data

data.text: Statements like CREATE TABLE and CREATE DATABASE are called *Data Definition Language* (DDL) — they define the structure. INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE are *Data Manipulation Language* (DML) — they change the data. In many organizations, only database administrators can run DDL, while developers have DML permissions.
